headings.text: What the official Kotlin example does
Enable Kotlin (and Compose) in your build
Java or Kotlin — which to use?

blocks.html:
Everything so far has been Java, because the canonical helloworld example is Java. But ATAK plugins can be written in Kotlin — a plugin is a normal Android app, and the ATAK API (though written in Java) is fully callable from Kotlin with seamless interop. The repo even ships a Kotlin example: **plugin-examples/plugintemplate-compose**, which builds its UI with Jetpack Compose in Kotlin.

What the official Kotlin example does

plugintemplate-compose mixes languages, which is a perfectly normal pattern:

  • Entry-point plumbing stays Java — PluginTemplateLifecycle, PluginTemplateTool, PluginTemplateMapComponent are .java (identical in shape to the classes on The plugin lifecycle).
  • The UI is Kotlin — PluginTemplateDropDownReceiver.kt renders with Compose.

You can go further and write every class in Kotlin; the example just shows the most common reason to reach for it (a modern, declarative UI).

Enable Kotlin (and Compose) in your build

Add the Kotlin Gradle plugin(s) and, if you want Compose, the Compose plugin + BOM. From plugintemplate-compose/app/build.gradle:

apply plugin: 'com.android.application'
apply plugin: 'atak-takdev-plugin'
apply plugin: 'org.jetbrains.kotlin.android'         // Kotlin
apply plugin: 'org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose'  // Compose (omit if not using it)

android {
    kotlinOptions { jvmTarget = JavaVersion.VERSION_1_8.toString() }
    buildFeatures.compose = true                     // omit if not using Compose
}

dependencies {
    def composeBom = platform('androidx.compose:compose-bom:2025.02.00')
    implementation(composeBom)
    implementation 'androidx.compose.material3:material3'
    implementation 'androidx.compose.ui:ui'
    implementation 'androidx.compose.ui:ui-tooling-preview'
    debugImplementation 'androidx.compose.ui:ui-tooling'
}

For Kotlin without Compose, keep only org.jetbrains.kotlin.android and drop the compose plugin, buildFeatures.compose, and the Compose dependencies. Everything else about the build (Build, install & run) is unchanged.

A Kotlin + Compose DropDownReceiver (real example)

This is the example's actual UI receiver — the Kotlin counterpart of the Java one on Build a UI:

class PluginTemplateDropDownReceiver(
    mapView: MapView?,
    private val pluginContext: Context
) : DropDownReceiver(mapView), OnStateListener {

    override fun onReceive(context: Context, intent: Intent) {
        val action = intent.action ?: return

        val view = ComposeView(ComposeContext(mapView.context, pluginContext)).apply {
            setViewCompositionStrategy(ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnDetachedFromWindow)
            setContent {
                MaterialTheme(colorScheme = darkColorScheme()) {
                    Row {
                        Icon(
                            painter = painterResource(id = R.drawable.ic_launcher),
                            contentDescription = null,
                            modifier = Modifier.size(40.dp),
                        )
                        Text("PluginTemplate")
                    }
                }
            }
        }

        if (action == SHOW_PLUGIN) {
            showDropDown(view, HALF_WIDTH, FULL_HEIGHT, FULL_WIDTH, HALF_HEIGHT, false, this)
        }
    }

    public override fun disposeImpl() {}
    override fun onDropDownClose() {}
    override fun onDropDownVisible(v: Boolean) {}
    override fun onDropDownSizeChanged(width: Double, height: Double) {}
    override fun onDropDownSelectionRemoved() {}

    companion object {
        const val SHOW_PLUGIN = "com.atakmap.android.plugintemplate.SHOW_PLUGIN"
    }
}

What carries over from the Java page, and what's new:

  • Same API. DropDownReceiver(mapView), OnStateListener, and the identical showDropDown(view, HALF_WIDTH, FULL_HEIGHT, FULL_WIDTH, HALF_HEIGHT, false, this) call — only the syntax differs.
  • Compose UI. Instead of inflating an XML layout, you build a ComposeView and setContent { … } with Material3. (Traditional XML layouts via PluginLayoutInflater still work in Kotlin too.)
  • The action constant lives in a companion object.

The two-Context rule, Compose edition

The plugin-vs-MapView context rule from How ATAK plugins work gets a Compose-specific wrinkle: ComposeView needs the plugin context to resolve your resources, but the host application context for its internals. The example solves it with a small ContextWrapper:

private class ComposeContext(val hostContext: Context, val pluginContext: Context) :
    ContextWrapper(pluginContext) {                          // resources from the plugin
    override fun getApplicationContext(): Context =
        hostContext.applicationContext                       // app context from the host
}

Use it as ComposeView(ComposeContext(mapView.context, pluginContext)), as above.

Kotlin for the plumbing too (optional)

The official example keeps the entry point in Java, but it translates directly — the API is identical. For instance, the Kotlin equivalent of the entry point from The plugin lifecycle:

// Kotlin equivalent of the Java HelloWorldLifecycle (AbstractPlugin entry point)
class HelloWorldLifecycle(serviceController: IServiceController) : AbstractPlugin(
    serviceController,
    HelloWorldTool(
        serviceController.getService(PluginContextProvider::class.java).pluginContext
    ),
    HelloWorldMapComponent(),
)

Note the idiomatic interop: getService(PluginContextProvider::class.java) for the Java Class<T> argument, and .pluginContext calling the Java getPluginContext() getter as a property.

Java or Kotlin — which to use?

  • Kotlin gives you null-safety and far less boilerplate, and interops cleanly with the Java ATAK API. You can adopt it file-by-file.
  • Compose is a viable, modern way to build the DropDown UI (the example proves it), but plain Android XML layouts remain fully supported.
  • Java is what every core example except plugintemplate-compose uses, so it has the most copy-paste reference material.
